messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi has come to believe that his own kitchen is a hostile space. The final straw was last Tuesday evening, when a sliver of garlic, forgotten in the hot oil for a moment too long, sent a plume of acrid smoke into the air. The smell, sharp and stinging, was a key turning a lock in his mind. He was no longer in his quiet Chicago apartment but back in the flat he had shared with David six months ago. The same burnt smell filled his nostrils, thick and suffocating, just as it had that night when the pot of jollof rice had scorched on the stove, completely forgotten. With the smell came the memory, not as a thought but as a full-body reenactment. A phantom bloom of pain flared across his ribs, a dull, deep ache exactly where the kicks had landed. The terror was the most immediate part—a cold, paralyzing wave that started in his stomach and seized his lungs, the same helpless fear he felt when David, his breath sour with whiskey, had pinned him against the wall.

That night had been the end. The argument had started over something trivial, but it had twisted into something ugly when David, his voice slurring, had sneered, “You’re just like them, aren’t you? So weak, just like your family.” The comment about his family, who had sacrificed so much for him to build a life here, had been the spark. The violence that followed was a blur of motion and pain, punctuated by the smell of burnt rice and the overpowering scent of alcohol every time David shouted in his face. Now, standing in his own kitchen, Kofi dropped the pan into the sink with a clatter, his heart hammering against his ribs. He felt dirty, as if the memory itself had left a film on his skin that no amount of scrubbing could remove.

In the months since he left, Kofi has felt like a ghost haunting his own life. The man he was before—a confident curriculum designer, praised for his creative and engaging educational models—seems like a stranger to him now. He sees that former self in old photos, smiling easily, and feels a profound sense of loss. The person he has become is unrecognisable, a man who flinches at the smell of hand sanitizer at the office and who has to plan his route home from work to avoid walking past the bars where the scent of stale beer spills onto the sidewalk. He feels a constant, simmering anger at the injustice of it all. David faced no consequences. He was still out there, living his life, while Kofi was trapped in this sensory prison, ambushed by the smell of a colleague’s lunchtime whiskey-glaze salmon or a casual question about his family.

His work, once a source of pride, has become a struggle. During a brainstorming session last month, a coworker asked him about his family’s traditions to inform a module on cultural heritage. Kofi froze, David’s mocking words echoing in his head. He gave a clipped, noncommittal answer and spent the rest of the meeting staring at his laptop, the creative part of his brain feeling locked away and inaccessible. He has started declining all social invitations, especially after-work drinks, fabricating excuses that he knows sound flimsy to his colleagues. The isolation is a heavy blanket, but it feels safer than the risk of another memory ambush.

He decided to seek help after an incident at work where someone burned popcorn in the breakroom microwave. The smell flooded the open-plan office. For Kofi, it was the same acrid, choking scent from that night. He felt the terror rise, the ghost pain in his side so sharp he gasped. He could almost smell the whiskey on David’s breath again. He fled to the men’s room, locking himself in a stall and pressing his forehead against the cool metal, breathing through the panic until the shaking subsided. It was the public nature of the collapse, the sheer humiliation of his own reaction, that clarified things. He could not live like this anymore. He is not sure if the man he was is someone he can ever be again, but he holds onto a desperate hope that he can at least learn to feel clean again, to stand in his own kitchen without fear.
